Publication Trends, Topic Dynamics, and Open Access Patterns

1. Publication Volume & Temporal Distribution

Analyze the monthly and yearly distribution of publications, noting the natural skew toward 2024 due to PubMed indexing lag. Present volume trends over time and discuss seasonality or acceleration patterns.

Key Finding: The distribution is heavily skewed toward 2024, consistent with PubMed indexing lag. January 2024 dominates (1,665 publications), while 2025 and 2026 volumes show the expected progressive decline as indexing catches up. The monthly pattern within each year reveals a pronounced January surge, likely reflecting end-of-year publication backlogs and editorial scheduling.

Seasonality Observations

Within 2024 (the only year with near-complete monthly coverage), the publication volume exhibits a strong January peak followed by a sharp February decline and a gradual tapering through year-end. This pattern is consistent with known academic publishing cycles: end-of-year submission surges, editorial processing over the holiday period, and a resulting January publication cluster. The 2025 monthly distribution, while provisional, shows a more even spread, with notable volume in December 2025 (94 publications) — the highest non-January month observed.

2. Geographic Landscape of Biomedical Research

Identify the top contributing countries by publication count, examine how geographic contributions shift over the 2024–2026 window, and highlight any emerging or declining national research presences.

Key Finding: China leads biomedical research output with 1,082 publications (22.1% of total), followed by the USA at 539 (11.0%). The top 10 countries together contribute 53.7% of all publications, indicating moderate geographic concentration. Notably, China's share of publication volume is roughly double that of the USA in this dataset.

Geographic Shifts (2024 vs. 2025–2026)

China's share of 2024 publications was 23.8% (935 of 3,924) and decreased in the provisional 2025 data to 13.7% (101 of 737), though this likely reflects indexing lag rather than a true decline. India shows an increasing share in provisional 2025 data (8.0% vs. 3.3% in 2024), which may indicate growing research output. Iran has the highest open access rate among top-10 countries at 86.9%, while the "Unknown" country category has the lowest at 25.0%.

Strategic Note: The "Unknown" country category (144 publications, 2.9%) represents a data quality gap that complicates geographic analysis. Analysts should note that some country names are non-standardized (e.g., "PR China", "People's Republic of China" alongside "China"), requiring normalization for accurate comparisons.

3. Research Topic & MeSH Keyword Analysis

Examine the most prevalent major topics and MeSH keywords, identify trending or emerging research areas across the time period, and note any topic shifts between years.

Key Finding: COVID-19 remains the dominant MeSH major topic (43 publications), though its volume is concentrated in 2024 and declines sharply in 2025–2026. Chronic disease topics — Diabetes Mellitus Type 2 (24), Breast Neoplasms (17), Alzheimer Disease (15) — form a consistent research core. Emerging areas include gastrointestinal microbiome research and long noncoding RNA, both showing sustained interest across the period.

4. Open Access Adoption & Journal Landscape

Quantify the proportion of open-access vs. closed-access publications, identify leading journals by volume, and assess whether open-access rates are changing over time or vary by country and research type.

Key Finding: The overall open access rate is {oa_rate:.1f}%, meaning nearly two-thirds of publications are available via PubMed Central. The OA rate increased from 64.1% in 2024 to 74.1% in 2025 (+10 percentage points), before dipping to 53.8% in early 2026 — a pattern that may reflect early-indexing bias (subscription journals often index faster than OA journals for early-year articles).

Open Access by Research Type

Preprints have 100% open access (by definition), while Case Reports lead traditional publication types at 83.2% OA. Randomized Controlled Trials have the lowest OA rate at 43.1%, a concerning finding for evidence-based medicine accessibility.

Scientific Reports leads in publication volume (82 articles, 100% OA), followed by Heliyon (76, 100% OA) and Cureus (69, 91.3% OA). The dominance of fully-OA journals in the top ranks reflects the growing prominence of open-access publishing platforms in biomedical research. Traditional subscription-model journals show lower OA rates, though many now offer hybrid OA options.

Policy Insight: The upward OA trend (64% → 74% from 2024 to 2025) aligns with global policy momentum toward open science. If sustained, this trajectory could see OA rates approaching 80% within 2–3 years. Funders and institutions should prepare infrastructure for a predominantly OA publishing ecosystem.

Collaboration Intensity

The author count distribution reveals several patterns:

  • Median 6 authors per paper — consistent across all three years, suggesting stable collaboration norms.
  • Italy leads in collaboration intensity (median 8 authors) among top countries, followed by China and Brazil (median 7). India and Iran show lower medians (5 authors).
  • Preprints have the highest author counts (median 9, mean 12.1), consistent with large multi-center studies and consortia that preprint before journal submission.
  • Editorials average just 2.9 authors, reflecting their nature as individually or small-team authored opinion pieces.
Strategic Note: The stability of median author counts across years (6.0 in all three years) suggests collaboration intensity is an established norm rather than an accelerating trend. However, the heavy right tail (max 115 authors) indicates that "hyper-authorship" — driven by large international consortia and genomics studies — continues to coexist with smaller-team research.

6. Key Takeaways & Strategic Implications

Synthesize the most important findings into actionable insights for research policy, funding prioritization, and institutional strategy.

  1. China and the USA dominate biomedical research output, but the landscape is diversifying. China (22.1%) and the USA (11.0%) together account for one-third of indexed publications. India, Iran, and South Korea show growing research presence. Funding agencies should monitor shifts in the geographic balance of research output, particularly as indexing lag resolves for 2025–2026 data. Strategic implication: International collaboration policies and bilateral research agreements should account for these shifting concentrations.
  2. Open Access adoption is trending upward but unevenly distributed. The OA rate rose from 64.1% (2024) to 74.1% (2025), a 10-point increase. However, Randomized Controlled Trials — critical for evidence-based medicine — have the lowest OA rate (43.1%). Preprints achieve 100% OA by definition but represent only 0.8% of indexed output. Strategic implication: Mandate OA for publicly funded clinical trials; invest in preprint infrastructure while maintaining quality controls.
  3. COVID-19 research is declining; chronic disease and microbiome research are steady-state priorities. COVID-19 was the top MeSH topic (43 publications) but its volume is concentrated in 2024. Diabetes, oncology, Alzheimer's, and gastrointestinal microbiome research show consistent presence, suggesting durable funding needs. Strategic implication: Rebalance funding from emergency COVID-19 programs toward sustained investment in chronic disease and emerging areas like the microbiome.
  4. Collaboration intensity (median 6 authors) is stable, but "hyper-authorship" is notable. The median author count of 6 has been consistent across 2024–2026, but the distribution stretches to 115 authors, driven by large consortia. Strategic implication: Credit and attribution systems must adapt to hyper-authored works; traditional "first author / last author" models strain under 50+ author papers.
  5. Journal Articles dominate (83.6%), but Review articles and Case Reports remain significant. Reviews (8.3%) and Case Reports (3.9%) together represent over 12% of output. Reviews show slightly higher OA rates than journal articles. Strategic implication: Ensure review articles and case reports are included in OA mandates and repository policies, not just original research articles.
  6. PubMed indexing lag makes real-time trend analysis difficult. The 2024 dominance (80.3% of records) is a known artifact of PubMed's indexing process. Real-time monitoring of 2025–2026 trends requires normalized metrics and caution in interpretation. Strategic implication: Invest in alternative data sources (preprint servers, institutional repositories) to complement PubMed for real-time research landscape monitoring.
  7. Geographic data quality gaps exist. The "Unknown" country category (2.9% of records) and non-standardized country names complicate geographic analysis. Strategic implication: Advocate for improved affiliation metadata standards in PubMed submissions; develop automated country-name normalization pipelines.

Bottom Line for Decision-Makers

The biomedical research ecosystem is characterized by geographic concentration with signs of diversification, accelerating open access adoption, and stable collaboration norms. The key strategic priorities are: (1) preparing infrastructure and policy for an increasingly OA-dominated publishing landscape; (2) monitoring the geographic rebalancing of research output as 2025–2026 indexing matures; and (3) ensuring that OA benefits extend to the publication types — particularly clinical trials — where accessibility has the greatest impact on evidence-based practice.
